segments.t: The integrated SFTP Manager provides a graphical file manager for transferring files between your local machine and remote servers via SFTP. It features a dual-panel layout, full file operations support, and seamless integration with the Snippet Editor for remote file editing.
You can open the SFTP Manager in two ways:

KTPH006Menu:KTPH007 KTPH008Connections → SFTP-Client...KTPH009 (KTPH010KTPH000KTPH011+KTPH012KTPH001KTPH013+KTPH014KTPH002KTPH015, on macOS KTPH016KTPH003KTPH017+KTPH018KTPH004KTPH019+KTPH020KTPH005KTPH021). With a connected terminal tab in front, it opens on that tab's focused pane, as KTPH022Open SFTP HereKTPH023 does; otherwise you pick a connection first.

KTPH000From a terminal:KTPH001 KTPH002Connections → Open SFTP HereKTPH003, KTPH004Open SFTP hereKTPH005 in a terminal tab's right-click menu, or KTPH006Open SFTP hereKTPH007 in a pane's right-click menu. The command palette finds it too. See KTPH008Opening from a terminal tabKTPH009.
KTPH000Dashboard:KTPH001 right-click a connected session KTPH004 KTPH002SFTP-Client...KTPH003
If the connection uses a temporary SSH key that has expired, you will be prompted to enter a new key before the connection can proceed.

KTPH000Open SFTP HereKTPH001 opens the SFTP Manager on the SSH session the terminal pane already has, so there is no second login: no second password or MFA prompt, no second hop through a jump server, and no CyberArk access reason asked again. It uses the pane you are typing in (or the pane you right-clicked), and in a split tab whose pane runs another connection it opens as that pane's user and server, not the tab's.

The remote side starts in the folder the shell is in: the one the shell reports (OSC 7 or the korTTY agent hook), else the folder shown in the prompt, else the folder of your last KTPH000. KTPH001 and relative folders are resolved against your home folder. If that folder no longer exists, the login folder is shown and the status bar says so. Two cases start in the login folder on purpose, with a note in the status bar: a pane where a different session is active (after KTPH002, KTPH003 or a nested KTPH004), because its folder belongs to another user or host, and a connection with a shell startup command, which may switch user before the first prompt.

Each pane gets its own SFTP tab, so two panes of the same server can be browsed side by side; choosing KTPH000Open SFTP HereKTPH001 again for the same pane selects its tab. A tab opened from KTPH002Connections → SFTP-Client...KTPH003 with a connection picked is still one per connection, and the two kinds never replace each other.

Such a tab copies at most two files at once, even when KTPH000Settings → SFTP ManagerKTPH001 allows more, so the terminal on the same session stays responsive. Closing the tab never closes the terminal. When the terminal's session ends, or the pane is closed or now runs another user or host, the tab shows KTPH002DisconnectedKTPH003 with KTPH004ReconnectKTPH005, which uses the pane's session again once it is back, and KTPH006Separate loginKTPH007, which closes the tab and opens one with its own login for the pane's connection.

When the pane has no SSH session to share (a Mosh or local shell tab), or the server or a proxy refuses SFTP on it, korTTY opens an SFTP tab with its own login for the pane's connection instead, as before. A saved KTPH000projectKTPH001 restores such a tab as an ordinary SFTP tab with its own login, in the folders it was in.

For a quick look without opening a tab, KTPH001View → Remote Files SidebarKTPH002 docks a file list beside the terminal panes that lists the folder the focused SSH pane's shell is in, over that pane's session, and follows the shell as you KTPH000. The sidebar never types into the terminal; its uploads, downloads and drops go through the KTPH003transfer listKTPH004 after a confirmation that names the server folder. See KTPH005Remote files sidebarKTPH006.
The SFTP Manager uses a KTPH000two-panel layoutKTPH001 for easy side-by-side file management:

The panel you work in is the KTPH002active panelKTPH003: clicking anywhere in a panel, or moving the keyboard focus into it, frames it in the accent colour, colours the dot before its title and draws its selected rows in the accent colour. The other panel keeps its selection, drawn muted, so you can see at a glance which list your last click and keys such as KTPH004KTPH000KTPH005 and KTPH006KTPH001KTPH007 act on.

Each panel has its own row of buttons under its list, and every button acts on the panel it sits in: KTPH000RefreshKTPH001, KTPH002New FolderKTPH003, KTPH004DeleteKTPH005, KTPH006RightsKTPH007, KTPH008ArchiveKTPH009 and KTPH010EditKTPH011 in both rows, KTPH012UploadKTPH013 at the right end of the local row and KTPH014DownloadKTPH015 at the left end of the server row, where the two panels meet.

The eye button beside the home button of each panel shows or hides that panel's hidden entries: names starting with a dot, such as KTPH000 or KTPH001, and on the local side also files and folders the file system marks hidden (the hidden attribute on Windows). KTPH009KTPH003KTPH010+KTPH011KTPH004KTPH012+KTPH013KTPH005KTPH014 (KTPH015KTPH006KTPH016+KTPH017KTPH007KTPH018+KTPH019KTPH008KTPH020 on Windows and Linux) does the same for the list that has the keyboard focus, as in the macOS Finder. Each panel remembers its choice for the next SFTP tab; until you hide them, hidden entries are shown. The parent entry KTPH002 always stays, and the search field filters what is left.

The path of each panel is shown as clickable folders; click one to go there. To type a path instead, click the empty part of the bar or press KTPH006KTPH000KTPH007+KTPH008KTPH001KTPH009 (KTPH010KTPH002KTPH011+KTPH012KTPH003KTPH013 on Windows and Linux) in the panel; KTPH014KTPH004KTPH015 goes there, and KTPH016KTPH005KTPH017 returns to the folders. When the path is wider than the bar, its end stays visible.

A line under each list counts its entries (while the search field narrows the list, how many of all are shown), the selected entries with their size, and the hidden entries the eye button hides. The KTPH000SizeKTPH001 column is right-aligned, and hovering over a date shows it in full.
Both panels display the same columns, all of which are sortable by clicking the column header:
A type icon: a folder, or a file icon chosen by the file name (code, image, archive, document, other)
File size in human-readable format; a folder shows — until KTPH000Calculate sizeKTPH001 measured it. Sorting uses the exact byte count within each group of the KTPH002sort orderKTPH003
Owner name (local: from the file system; on the server: as the server sends it, or looked up there when it sends only the UID; see KTPH000Owner and group namesKTPH001)
Group name (local: from the file system; on the server: as the server sends it, or looked up there when it sends only the GID)
Whichever column you sort by, the entries stay in these groups:
KTPH001Parent directoryKTPH002 (KTPH000) — always at the top
KTPH002Hidden foldersKTPH003 — names starting with "." (e.g., KTPH000, KTPH001)

Click a column header to order the entries within each group by that column; clicking it again reverses that order, but never the order of the groups. By default the lists are sorted by the KTPH000TypeKTPH001 column, which orders each group by name; names sort without regard to upper and lower case. While a panel hides its KTPH002hidden filesKTPH003, groups 2 and 3 are left out.

Remote folders are read in the background, so the window stays responsive even for a folder with tens of thousands of entries. While a folder loads, a KTPH000Loading…KTPH001 indicator covers the remote list. The path field and the list switch to the new folder only once it has been read; if it cannot be read (it does not exist, or you lack the rights), an error is shown and the folder you were in stays.

Type a path into the remote KTPH008PathKTPH009 field and press KTPH010KTPH007KTPH011 to go there. KTPH000 and KTPH001 stand for your login directory on the server, and a path without a leading KTPH002 is taken relative to the folder shown; KTPH003 and KTPH004 are resolved, so KTPH005 opens the sibling folder KTPH006.

OpenSSH and other servers that speak SFTP version 3 send owners and groups only as numbers (UID and GID). korTTY then asks the server once for the names behind numbers it has not seen yet, with KTPH000, which also knows LDAP and other directory accounts, or from KTPH001 and KTPH002 where KTPH003 is missing. The names replace the numbers a moment after the list appears; the list never waits for them. KTPH004Set Owner/PermissionsKTPH005 is prefilled with the names too.
A server that cannot run commands (such as an account limited to SFTP) or that has not answered after 8 seconds keeps showing the numbers, and korTTY does not ask it again until you reconnect.

KTPH001Calculate sizeKTPH002 in the right-click menu of the server list measures the selected folders with KTPH000 on the server. The KTPH003SizeKTPH004 column shows the result for each folder and the status bar the total; sorting by KTPH005SizeKTPH006 then orders these folders by it. The figure is the disk space the files take, which can differ a little from the sum of their sizes. While the measurement runs, the same menu item reads KTPH007Stop calculating sizeKTPH008. The sizes are dropped when the list is read again.

When the server or the network ends the session, the status bar shows KTPH000Disconnected fromKTPH001 KTPH002hostKTPH003 with a KTPH004ReconnectKTPH005 button, and the remote actions are disabled. If the connection drops without the server saying so, the first remote action you try (Refresh, Upload, Download and so on) brings up the same state instead of doing nothing.

KTPH000ReconnectKTPH001 opens a new session with the same credentials and lists the folder you were in. The server's host key is checked as on the first connect: an unchanged key connects without a prompt, a changed key is still blocked.

SFTP Manager tabs are saved with a KTPH000projectKTPH001. Opening the project with KTPH002Auto-ReconnectKTPH003 reconnects each tab at the local and remote folders it was in when you saved. A folder that no longer exists opens the home folder instead; on the remote side the status bar says so.
KTPH000CompareKTPH001 in the local row of buttons, and KTPH002Compare...KTPH003 in the right-click menu of both lists, looks at what is selected:
KTPH000Two filesKTPH001, two selected in the active panel or one in each panel, open side by side; see KTPH002Comparing two filesKTPH003.

KTPH000Two foldersKTPH001: a local and a server folder are compared in the bar above the lists, and both panels go into them; two folders on the same side open in a window of their own; see KTPH002Two folders on the same sideKTPH003.
KTPH000Nothing like thatKTPH001: the local folder shown is compared with the server folder shown.
A file and a folder cannot be compared with each other; the status bar says so.

The two files open side by side in a window with their changes marked, like the comparison of two snippets in the snippet manager. The line above them counts the added and removed lines. Files larger than 4 MB and files that are not text (a NUL byte near the start) are not compared. A file on the server is read through SFTP; that needs a connection and is refused when your organization does not let server files be loaded into an editor. In a folder comparison, a double-click on a file that exists on both sides opens the two files the same way.

KTPH000Ask AIKTPH001 opens a panel beside the two files and widens the window for it, so the files stay side by side. Pick a prepared question (where the files differ, what the differences do, or what could be improved in the right-hand version) or write your own, choose the AI profile when there are several, and click KTPH002AskKTPH003; the button next to it stops the request. Both files with line numbers and their unified diff go to the profile, and secrets it recognizes, such as keys and passwords, are masked first unless the profile runs on this computer. The answer appears below the question, and the request counts towards the profile's usage like any other AI request. This suits shell scripts and configuration files, where a changed line can change what a service does.

KTPH005A-KTPH006 and KTPH007A+KTPH008 next to the title of the panel make the question and the answers smaller or larger, as do KTPH009KTPH000KTPH010+KTPH011KTPH001KTPH012 and KTPH013KTPH002KTPH014+KTPH015KTPH003KTPH016 (KTPH017KTPH004KTPH018 on macOS); korTTY remembers the size for the next comparison. When the panel is in the way, the button KTPH019✕KTPH020 at its top right hides it and gives its width back to the files; KTPH021Ask AIKTPH022 shows it again with the last answer.
KTPH000Ask AIKTPH001 can be clicked only when the AI features are on, your organization allows AI requests, and at least one AI profile exists; otherwise hovering over it tells you what is missing.
A new file from both filesKTPH000

At the top of the AI panel, KTPH000AskKTPH001 and KTPH002New fileKTPH003 choose what the AI does. With KTPH004New fileKTPH005, the AI writes a new, third file from the two as you describe it: pick a prepared instruction such as KTPH006The best of bothKTPH007 or KTPH008Improve the right fileKTPH009, or write your own, and click KTPH010Create fileKTPH011. The AI first lists what it changed and then sends the complete file. The comparison then shows the right file against the new one, and the list above the files picks the two files it shows: left and right, right and the new file, or left and the new file. An answer without a complete file, for example one that was cut off, is shown but not taken as the file.
Below the answer, KTPH000New fileKTPH001 offers what to do with the file:
Compares the new file with the right file again

Asks where the file goes, on the server or on this computer, and at which path; the place of the right-hand file is proposed, since the new file is meant to replace it, and KTPH000Browse...KTPH001 picks another place with a click

Opens the new file in the snippet editor. There you can edit it, give it a name and a category, and keep it in the Snippet Manager with KTPH000Save as snippetKTPH001. KTPH002Replace the right fileKTPH003 and KTPH004Save as...KTPH005 in the editor save the edited file instead

On this computer, KTPH002Browse...KTPH003 opens the save dialog of the system. On the server, it lists the folders and files of the server: a double-click opens a folder (KTPH000 is the folder above), a click on a file takes its name, and the name can also be typed. A folder typed into the path field above the list opens with KTPH004KTPH001KTPH005.

If the file already exists, korTTY asks before overwriting it and first keeps the previous version next to it as KTPH000, unless you turn off KTPH001Keep an existing file as .bak firstKTPH002. Overwriting keeps the permissions of the file, and the backup gets the same ones, so a configuration that only its owner may read stays that way. Saving on the server needs a connection and is not offered when your organization keeps server files read-only in editors or turns off file transfer. When the new file is saved over one of the two compared files, the comparison shows what that file holds now.

When a local folder is compared with a server folder (the two shown, or two selected ones), all subfolders are included. It first asks for patterns to leave out, one per line, such as KTPH000 or KTPH001. Then both folders are read in the background; the bar above the lists counts what has been read, and a button at its end stops the comparison. Names, sizes and modification times are compared, and times less than 2 seconds apart count as the same, because SFTP version 3 keeps whole seconds. Symbolic links are left out on both sides, and more than 100,000 entries on one side stop the comparison.

The result stays in the bar above the lists: how many entries exist only on one side, are newer on one side, are different (equally old but of another size, or a file on one side and a folder on the other), and are the same. The rows take colours, each seen from its own side: green only here, orange newer here, red different, and dimmed when the same or older here. A folder is red when something inside it differs, and the colours follow you into the subfolders of the compared folders. KTPH000Differences onlyKTPH001 hides what is the same; KTPH002Compare againKTPH003 (the arrow) and KTPH004End the comparisonKTPH005 (the cross) sit at the end of the bar. A double-click on a compared file that exists on both sides shows the two files side by side.

KTPH000To the serverKTPH001 copies what is missing on the server, what is newer here, and what has the same age but another size; KTPH002To this computerKTPH003 does the same in the other direction. A dialog lists what is copied and how much first. Files that exist on the target are replaced without a question per file, and every copy keeps the modification time of its original, so the next comparison finds the two the same. A newer file on the target stays as it is, and so does a path that is a file on one side and a folder on the other.

The dialog also has a checkbox, off by default, that deletes what exists only on the target; after a second confirmation, it is deleted for good. The copies run in the KTPH000transfer listKTPH001, and the folders are compared again once they are done. When your organization switches file transfer off, both buttons only show the reason in the status bar.
Two folders on the same sideKTPH000

Two local folders, or two folders on the server, are compared the same way, with the same patterns to leave out, but the result opens in a window of its own: the panels can only colour a local folder against a server folder. The window lists every path with how it compares, such as KTPH000Only rightKTPH001 or KTPH002Newer on the leftKTPH003, and its size and time on both sides, with KTPH004Differences onlyKTPH005 ticked at first. A double-click on a file that exists on both sides shows the two files side by side. Synchronizing is not offered here.

A name for KTPH004RenameKTPH005 or KTPH006New FolderKTPH007 must be a single entry in the folder shown: it may not be empty, KTPH000 or KTPH001, or contain KTPH002 or KTPH003. The dialog stays open with an error until the name is usable.

The top of the archive dialog says what is archived and where: the computer (KTPH000ServerKTPH001 with the connection's name and user@host, or KTPH002This computerKTPH003 with its name), the folder shown, how many folders and files are selected, and their names. The archive is written on that same computer.

Before a server archive dialog opens, korTTY asks the server once which archive tools it has, and the status bar says so meanwhile. For a server that runs no commands (such as an account limited to SFTP) or that has not answered after 8 seconds, korTTY assumes that KTPH000 and KTPH001 are installed. For the estimated size of a server archive, the dialog measures the selected folders the same way as KTPH003Calculate sizeKTPH004, in the background, and adds them once KTPH002 answers; a folder it cannot measure is left out, and the dialog says so.

The dialog takes the format (ZIP, TAR.BZ2 or 7z; a format whose tool the server lacks is marked KTPH000not installedKTPH001), the archive's path and a compression level from none to best. Its other fields are optional:
KTPH003ExcludeKTPH004 — one pattern per line, such as KTPH000, KTPH001 or KTPH002; it exists in both panels.
KTPH000PasswordKTPH001 — local archives only. It is greyed out for TAR.BZ2, a format without encryption, and server archives get no password at all.

KTPH000Extract Here...KTPH001 in the remote context menu unpacks the selected archive on the server itself, so nothing is downloaded or uploaded. After you confirm, a progress window shows each step, and KTPH002CancelKTPH003 stops the extraction and removes what was already unpacked.

KTPH004Always a new folderKTPH005 — the files land in a new folder next to the archive, named after it without the extension (KTPH000 becomes KTPH001). If that name is taken, korTTY uses KTPH002, KTPH003 and so on; an existing file or folder is never overwritten or merged into.

KTPH002Checked before anything is writtenKTPH003 — korTTY first lists the archive and refuses it as a whole when an entry would land outside the new folder: an absolute path, KTPH000 that climbs above the folder, a drive letter such as KTPH001, a name with a line break, a device file, or a link whose target lies outside. Nothing is written in that case.

KTPH001Checked again after unpackingKTPH002 — the archive is unpacked into a hidden staging folder (KTPH000 plus random characters) that only you can open, without taking over the owners stored in the archive. korTTY then checks every symbolic link in it; if one points outside the folder, the staging folder is deleted and you get an error. Only a clean result is renamed to the new folder, so it appears complete or not at all.

KTPH004Tools on the serverKTPH005 — ZIP needs KTPH000, the tar formats KTPH001, and 7z KTPH002 or KTPH003. If the tool is missing, the error names it. With a tar other than GNU tar (for example BusyBox), archives with hard links are refused, because their targets cannot be checked.
KTPH000No passwordsKTPH001 — password-protected archives are refused with a message: the tools would need the password on the server's command line, where other users of the server can read it.

You can drag entries between the two panels, from your desktop into the SFTP Manager, and in small amounts from the server to your desktop. While you drag, the panel or the folder row that would take the drop is highlighted; dropping on a folder row puts the entries into that folder, dropping anywhere else into the folder shown.
Local rows onto the remote panel

Only for at most 20 files with at most 16 MB together, and no folders
A drag into the same panel does nothing; use KTPH000Copy to...KTPH001 or KTPH002RenameKTPH003 there.
Dragging from the server to the desktop

The desktop can only take files that already exist when the drag starts. korTTY therefore downloads the dragged remote files into a private temporary folder first, which can hold the window for up to 5 seconds. Folders, more than 20 files, more than 16 MB or a download that takes longer can only be dropped inside the window; the status bar says so, and you drop them on the local panel instead. A download that runs out of time stops in the middle of its file and deletes what it wrote, so it does not go on filling the temporary folder in the background. A link on the server counts as the file it points to, so a link to a large file is not offered to the desktop either. The temporary copies are deleted when you start the next drag or close the tab.
These keys work in both panels:
KTPH005KTPH000KTPH006 or KTPH007KTPH001KTPH008+KTPH009KTPH002KTPH010 (KTPH011KTPH003KTPH012+KTPH013KTPH004KTPH014 on macOS, in the list)
Type a path in the panel's path bar
KTPH006KTPH000KTPH007+KTPH008KTPH001KTPH009+KTPH010KTPH002KTPH011 (KTPH012KTPH003KTPH013+KTPH014KTPH004KTPH015+KTPH016KTPH005KTPH017 on Windows and Linux, in the list)

Upload copies the selected local files and folders into the remote folder that was shown when you clicked KTPH001UploadKTPH002; browsing elsewhere while it runs does not change the target. Upload stays disabled until the first remote folder has been listed, because the server does not expand KTPH000 itself.
KTPH000Uploading a folder again mergesKTPH001 into the existing remote folder: other remote files are kept, and for each file that already exists korTTY asks what to do (see below).
KTPH000Files are streamedKTPH001, so their size is not limited by memory; files larger than 2 GB upload like any other.

If the connection drops during an upload or download, the unfinished items fail as KTPH000Connection lostKTPH001 with one KTPH002DisconnectedKTPH003 state rather than an error dialog per file; after KTPH004ReconnectKTPH005, select them in the KTPH006transfer listKTPH007 and click KTPH008RetryKTPH009.

KTPH000Linked folders are not followed.KTPH001 A symbolic link to a file is transferred with the file's content; a link to a folder is skipped and named in the summary at the end, so a link loop cannot make a transfer run forever.

KTPH012Downloaded names stay inside the target folder.KTPH013 A server name such as KTPH000 or KTPH001 is refused. On Windows, names that Windows reserves for devices (KTPH002, KTPH003, KTPH004, KTPH005, KTPH006 to KTPH007, KTPH008 to KTPH009, also with an extension such as KTPH010) and names that end in a dot or a space or contain KTPH011 are refused too, because Windows would write them somewhere else or change them.

Uploads and downloads run in the background, by default three files at a time (KTPH000Settings → SFTP Manager → KTPH001Parallel transfersKTPH002KTPH003, 1 to 8), each over its own SFTP channel. A tab that borrows a terminal's session copies at most two at a time. The first transfer opens the KTPH004TransfersKTPH005 list at the bottom of the tab; the arrow on its left collapses it to its header. Each row is a file or folder you transferred, with its direction, a progress bar, the bytes so far, the speed and the time left; a folder row adds up the files in it. The status bar shows how many files of all running transfers are done and the overall speed, and says KTPH006Upload completeKTPH007 or KTPH008Download completeKTPH009 when a batch is finished.
Stops the selected rows; a cancelled file leaves no partial file behind, unless the settings keep it for a later resume
Starts the selected failed or cancelled rows again; for a folder, only what did not arrive
Stops every transfer, including an open KTPH000File already existsKTPH001 question
Removes the rows that are done, skipped or cancelled; failed rows stay for a retry

KTPH000Failures no longer open one error dialog per file.KTPH001 A failed file gets a red row of its own (also when it is inside a folder you transferred), the reason is in its KTPH002StateKTPH003 column, and once the batch is finished one summary window lists the failed files and the linked folders that were not followed. The summary does not block the tab.
KTPH000The lists follow the transfers.KTPH001 When files arrive in the folder a panel shows, that panel is listed again shortly afterwards; a folder you browsed away from is not.

KTPH001Files arrive complete or not at all.KTPH002 A file is first written as KTPH000 next to the target and gets its real name only once it is complete, so an interrupted transfer never leaves a half-written file under the real name. The one exception is replacing a server file that belongs to another user, which is written in place (see KTPH003When a file already existsKTPH004).

KTPH000Interrupted transfers continue where they stopped.KTPH001 After a failure or a lost connection, KTPH002RetryKTPH003 continues an unfinished file instead of starting over; see KTPH004Resuming interrupted transfersKTPH005.

KTPH000Closing the tab asks while transfers run.KTPH001 The tab's close button, KTPH002File KTPH014 Close TabKTPH003, KTPH004Close All TabsKTPH005, closing the window and quitting korTTY first ask KTPH006Cancel KTPH007nKTPH008 running transfers and close?KTPH009; KTPH010Keep tab openKTPH011 is the default and leaves every transfer running. Closing cancels the transfers that are not finished and deletes their partial files, unless KTPH012Settings → SFTP ManagerKTPH013 keeps the partial files of cancelled transfers. Finished or failed rows ask nothing, and the automatic closing of idle tabs waits until the transfers are done.

KTPH001Leftover partial filesKTPH002 are shown in italics, with a tooltip. KTPH003Remove leftover partial filesKTPH004 at the end of either panel's context menu deletes the KTPH000 files in the folder shown after a confirmation; partial files of transfers that are still running are left alone.

A transfer that fails, or whose connection is lost, keeps its KTPH000 file, and KTPH001RetryKTPH002 (after KTPH003ReconnectKTPH004, if the connection was lost) continues it from where it stopped. While it continues, its KTPH005StateKTPH006 column says KTPH007ContinuingKTPH008.

KTPH000Only when nothing has changed.KTPH001 korTTY remembers the size and modification time of the source when the transfer starts. If the source is different on the retry, the partial file is larger than the source, or the last 64 KB before the resume point no longer match the source, the partial file is removed and the file is copied from the beginning.

KTPH000Only your own partial files.KTPH001 On the server a partial file is continued only when it is still a plain file owned by the user you are logged in as; a link or a file of another user at that name is never written to. On your computer the partial file is never followed through a link either. A partial file korTTY did not leave for this very transfer (another tab, another computer or another user may be writing it right now) is neither continued nor removed: the transfer fails with a message naming the file, and you remove a real leftover with KTPH002Remove leftover partial filesKTPH003.

KTPH000Cancel removes the partial fileKTPH001 unless KTPH002Settings → SFTP Manager → KTPH003Keep the partial file when a transfer is cancelledKTPH004KTPH005 is on. With KTPH006Resume interrupted transfersKTPH007 switched off there, every unfinished partial file is removed and a retry always starts over.

KTPH001What korTTY stores.KTPH002 The remembered sizes and times are kept in KTPH000 in korTTY's configuration folder, readable only by you. An entry holds a fingerprint of the connection and the two paths, not the paths or host names themselves, and never file content; entries of transfers you never retried are dropped after 30 days. The file is not part of the configuration backup, because the partial files it describes stay on this computer and its servers.
KTPH000Leftover partial filesKTPH001 of transfers you gave up on can be removed with KTPH002Remove leftover partial filesKTPH003 in either panel's context menu (see KTPH004Transfer listKTPH005).

An upload or download never replaces an existing file silently. When the target folder already has an entry of the same name, korTTY shows KTPH000File already existsKTPH001 with the size and modification time of both sides (the later time is marked as newer) and these choices:
The existing file is replaced by the transferred one
The existing entry is left alone and this item is not transferred
The item is transferred under a free name with a number, such as KTPH000; a double extension stays together (KTPH001), and a dotfile gets the number at the end (KTPH002)
The rest of the batch stops; closing the dialog or pressing KTPH001KTPH000KTPH002 does the same

KTPH000Do this for all remaining conflicts of this kindKTPH001 answers every later conflict of the same kind in that batch without asking again. The kinds are kept apart: replacing all files never replaces a symbolic link or a folder.
KTPH000A folder onto a folder of the same name mergesKTPH001 without asking; only the files inside it can conflict.

KTPH000A symbolic link is never replaced.KTPH001 When the existing entry is a link, only KTPH002SkipKTPH003 and KTPH004Keep bothKTPH005 are offered, so a transfer cannot write through a link to a file somewhere else.
KTPH000A file and a folder cannot replace each other.KTPH001 When one side is a file and the other a folder, only KTPH002SkipKTPH003 and KTPH004Keep bothKTPH005 are offered.

KTPH000A file owned by another user is written in place.KTPH001 When the existing remote file belongs to another user, the dialog says so; replacing it writes into the file directly, so its owner and permissions stay as they are.

KTPH000One question at a time.KTPH001 When several files of a batch conflict at once, korTTY asks about one of them and waits with the others, so an answer for all of them arrives before the next question. Closing the tab answers an open question with KTPH002Cancel transferKTPH003.

KTPH000The question can be answered in advance.KTPH001 KTPH002Settings → SFTP Manager → KTPH003When the target already existsKTPH004KTPH005 can skip existing files or overwrite them without asking; links and file/folder mismatches are still asked about. An organization can set this choice for you.

On a computer whose disk ignores upper and lower case (the macOS and Windows default), a name that differs only in case counts as the same name, both for the question and for the numbered name KTPH000Keep bothKTPH001 picks.
When file transfer is turned off by your organizationKTPH000

An organization can switch file transfer off with its KTPH002enterprise policyKTPH003 (KTPH000). The SFTP Manager then still opens and browses the server, and renaming, deleting, permissions, archives, search and copying on the server keep working, but KTPH004UploadKTPH005, KTPH006DownloadKTPH007 and KTPH008RetryKTPH009 in the transfer list are greyed out, dragging files onto the server panel or server files onto the local panel is not accepted (the pointer shows no copy symbol), and remote files cannot be dragged to the desktop. Files from the desktop can still be dropped onto the local panel. Dropping files onto a terminal pane is refused the same way while you drag, and KTPH010Copy as file(s) to terminal directoryKTPH011 and KTPH012Copy folder to terminal directoryKTPH013 in the Snippet Manager are greyed out for SSH tabs. KTPH014Open SFTP HereKTPH015 still opens for browsing. JobScheduler jobs that upload, download or sync with SFTP, and rsync jobs, fail with the same message without connecting. Commands such as KTPH001 typed into a terminal are not affected.

The permissions field of KTPH003Set Owner/PermissionsKTPH004 and of the remote archive dialog accepts exactly three octal digits, such as KTPH000 or KTPH001; leave it empty (or unchanged) to keep the current mode. Anything else keeps the dialog open with an error, so no other text ever reaches KTPH002.

In KTPH002Set Owner/PermissionsKTPH003, a grid of checkboxes under the field shows the mode as read, write and execute for the owner, the group and others. Ticking a checkbox writes the three digits into the field, and typing three digits ticks the checkboxes. Beside the field the mode is spelled out as KTPH000 shows it (KTPH001), or as KTPH004unchangedKTPH005 while the field is empty. For a folder, execute means that the folder can be opened and what it contains can be reached.

KTPH001Set Owner/PermissionsKTPH002 also changes the user and the group of local files and folders; another owner usually needs administrator rights. KTPH003Apply recursively to directoriesKTPH004 skips symbolic links inside a folder, just like KTPH000. An unknown name or a refused change is reported with the name of the entry.
The KTPH000Edit in Snippet EditorKTPH001 action is enabled only for a single selected file. It is disabled for:
Local files are read directly from the local filesystem; remote files are downloaded through the active SFTP session into the editor.
When the file opens in the Snippet Editor, the full toolbar remains available, including:
The file-mode buttons provide these save choices:
KTPH000Overwrite remote fileKTPH001 (KTPH002Overwrite local fileKTPH003 for a file in the left panel) — writes the current editor content back to the original file
KTPH000Save as...KTPH001 — writes a new file at a place picked with a click: in the save dialog of the system for a local file, in the folders and files of the server for a remote file
KTPH000Save as snippetKTPH001 — stores the current content as a new Snippet Manager snippet without marking the source file as saved

An organization can restrict editing server files with the KTPH000 key of its KTPH003enterprise policyKTPH004. With KTPH001, remote files still open in the Snippet Editor and can be saved as a snippet, but KTPH005Overwrite fileKTPH006 and KTPH007Save as...KTPH008 are locked and their tooltip names the policy. With KTPH002, KTPH009Edit in Snippet EditorKTPH010 and KTPH011Open imageKTPH012 are disabled for remote files. Local files in the left panel are on your own computer and stay editable either way.

KTPH000Edit in External EditorKTPH001 (in the right-click menu of a server file and in the remote KTPH002EditKTPH003 menu) opens the selected server file in your own text editor and copies every save back to the server. Choose the editor under KTPH004KTPH005Settings → SFTP Manager → External editorKTPH006KTPH007; without one, macOS opens the file in the default text editor, Windows opens it with its edit verb (scripts go to Notepad), and Linux opens text files with the default application for text and asks for an editor command for any other file type.

KTPH007Local copyKTPH008 — the file is downloaded into a private folder named KTPH000 in the system temp folder that only you can open, under a cleaned-up name: characters other than letters, digits, KTPH001, KTPH002, KTPH003 and spaces become KTPH004, and Windows device names such as KTPH005 get a KTPH006 in front. A symbolic link is followed once and the file it points to is edited.

KTPH001Auto-uploadKTPH002 — korTTY checks the copy every second. About a second after you save, the new content is uploaded and the status bar says KTPH003UploadedKTPH004 with the file name; saving the same content again uploads nothing. The upload works like any other: through a KTPH000 file that keeps the file's permissions, or written in place when the file belongs to another user, so its owner stays.

KTPH000Remote editsKTPH001 — the list below the transfer list shows each file being edited, whether it waits for saves, uploads or was uploaded (with the time), and offers KTPH002Upload nowKTPH003 for editors whose saves are not noticed, and KTPH004StopKTPH005.

KTPH000ConflictsKTPH001 — before each upload korTTY checks that the server file is still the one it downloaded (size, time, owner and, up to 10 MB, the content). If someone else changed or deleted it, it asks: KTPH002Overwrite server fileKTPH003, KTPH004Save local copy as...KTPH005 (keeps your version on this computer and stops watching), KTPH006Stop watchingKTPH007 or KTPH008Decide laterKTPH009 (keeps watching; nothing is uploaded until the next save or KTPH010Upload nowKTPH011).

KTPH000CleanupKTPH001 — KTPH002StopKTPH003, closing the SFTP tab and quitting korTTY delete the local copy. When the connection is lost before your last save was uploaded, korTTY first offers KTPH004Save copy as...KTPH005. Folders a crash left behind are removed at the next start once they are a day old.

The editor is always started directly, never through a shell or as the file's default application, so a downloaded script never runs. With the KTPH003enterprise policyKTPH004's KTPH000 the file opens but saves stay on your computer and the list says so; KTPH001 or KTPH002 grey out KTPH005Edit in External EditorKTPH006.

KTPH001Open With → Edit as Root (sudo)...KTPH002 (in the right-click menu of a server file, and KTPH003Edit as Root (sudo)...KTPH004 in the remote KTPH005EditKTPH006 menu) opens a file that only root may change, such as a configuration file under KTPH000, in your own editor, the same way as KTPH007Editing in your own editorKTPH008. The row in KTPH009Remote editsKTPH010 carries a KTPH011sudoKTPH012 badge.

KTPH002PasswordKTPH003 — korTTY first tries KTPH000, so with KTPH001 or a still-valid sudo ticket nothing is asked. Otherwise it asks for your password in a masked dialog. When the KTPH004JobSchedulerKTPH005 has a sudo password saved for the server or its group, the dialog offers to use it for this server from now on; korTTY never uses it without that choice, and unticking the box later takes it back. The password is kept only while the file is being edited, is handed to sudo only when sudo actually asks for it, and is wiped when you stop. It never appears in a command line, the log, an error message or the session journal.
KTPH001ReadingKTPH002 — the file is read with KTPH000 straight into the private local copy; nothing is written on the server for that.

KTPH000SavingKTPH001 — each save travels to the server over the connection, into a staging folder that root creates and owns, and only after its size and SHA-256 match is it written into the file itself. The file keeps its inode, owner, permissions, ACLs and SELinux label, and a broken transfer never leaves it half written. The staging folder is removed in every case. Before each save korTTY reads the file again as root; if someone else changed it meanwhile, the same conflict question as above appears.

KTPH000LinksKTPH001 — when the path is a symbolic link, or leads through a folder that is one, korTTY shows where the file really is and edits it there only after you confirm. Right before every read and write, root checks again that the file is no link and its folder is still the same real folder.

KTPH000RefusedKTPH001 — a file in a folder you can write to without sudo, or anywhere below such a folder, is not edited as root, because anything running as you could replace the file or a folder on its way in the meantime; the message names that folder, and you edit the file normally. Files larger than 64 MB are refused too.
KTPH001JournalKTPH002 — when a terminal on the same connection records a KTPH003session journalKTPH004, it gets one line, KTPH000 and the path; never the content.

KTPH007What the server needsKTPH008 — KTPH000, a POSIX KTPH001 with KTPH002, KTPH003 and KTPH004, and KTPH005 or KTPH006 for the content check. Without either hash tool korTTY still compares the size before it writes, but cannot compare the content.

KTPH005Servers with KTPH000KTPH006 — when the server's sudo configuration contains KTPH001, sudo refuses to run without a terminal, and korTTY says KTPH007sudo on this server requires a terminal (requiretty), and korTTY never runs sudo with oneKTPH008. korTTY does not work around this by opening a terminal: a terminal changes the bytes passing through it (line endings, control characters) and echoes what it is sent, so neither the file nor the password would arrive intact and unseen. An administrator can lift the rule for your account with a line such as KTPH002 (edited with KTPH003); until then, edit the file in a terminal tab, for example with KTPH004.
The KTPH004enterprise policyKTPH005 can switch the feature off with KTPH000; it is also greyed out while KTPH001 is denied or KTPH002 is not KTPH003.

The search field above each list filters the folder shown as you type, without leaving it; the parent entry KTPH000 stays visible. korTTY evaluates the wildcards itself, the same way for local and remote names. A pattern with a wildcard has to match the whole name, ignoring case:
KTPH000 finds all log files, KTPH001 all names starting with "backup"
One of the listed characters; KTPH000 or KTPH001 one that is not listed
KTPH000 finds names starting with a or b
KTPH000 finds Python and shell files
Text without a wildcard matches anywhere in the name, ignoring case: KTPH000 finds KTPH001. A pattern that cannot be read, such as an unclosed KTPH002, is searched for as plain text.

Check KTPH004Include subfoldersKTPH005 next to the remote search field and press KTPH006KTPH000KTPH007 to search the remote folder shown and every folder below it, with the same wildcards and the same case-insensitive matching. The remote list switches to the results: each hit shows its path below the searched folder, and the line above the list counts the hits while the search runs and says how it ended, for example KTPH008120 resultsKTPH009 or KTPH0105000 results, stopped at limitKTPH011. Double-click a hit, or select it and press KTPH012KTPH001KTPH013, to open its folder with the hit selected. KTPH014Back to folderKTPH015 returns to the folder listing, and KTPH016KTPH002KTPH017 in the search field stops a running search (a second KTPH018KTPH003KTPH019 leaves the results).
Folder levels below the searched folder

When the server lets korTTY run commands and has KTPH000, the search runs there and only the matching paths travel over the connection; otherwise korTTY walks the folders over SFTP, which is slower and stops after reading 200,000 entries. Symbolic links are listed but never followed, so a link that points back up the tree cannot make the search loop. KTPH003Stay on this file systemKTPH004 (on by default, and only with KTPH005Include subfoldersKTPH006) keeps KTPH001 out of other mounted file systems such as network shares and KTPH002; the walk over SFTP cannot tell file systems apart. Folders you cannot read are skipped. The search only reads names on the server, so it stays available when an enterprise policy blocks file transfers.
